panel_start, panel_end = panel.index.min(), panel.index.max()

Each raw SMARD series’ own coverage (dark bars), against the fixed
chronological split used by every baseline model (see
docs/modeling_plan.md): pv and wind_onshore have several years more
history than wind_offshore and load, which only start once the DE-LU
market area itself does (2018-10) — see docs/data_sources.md. The
combined panel used for modeling is trimmed to the common overlap, so
training only ever starts at the latest of the four start dates.



Figure 1:Raw per-series data availability (dark bars) against the train /
validation / test split (background bands) used by every baseline model.

availability = pd.DataFrame(
    [
        {
            "target": name,
            "start": pd.read_parquet(paths.smard_raw_file(name)).index.min(),
            "end": pd.read_parquet(paths.smard_raw_file(name)).index.max(),
        }
        for name in TARGETS

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 4))

ax.axvspan(panel_start, val_start, color="#86b6ef", alpha=0.35, zorder=1, label="Train")
ax.axvspan(val_start, test_start, color="#3987e5", alpha=0.35, zorder=1, label="Validation")
ax.axvspan(test_start, panel_end, color="#184f95", alpha=0.35, zorder=1, label="Test (reserved)")

y_positions = range(len(availability))
for y, row in zip(y_positions, availability.itertuples()):
    ax.barh(y, row.end - row.start, left=row.start, height=0.5, color="#0b0b0b", zorder=2, label="Data available" if y == 0 else None)

ax.set_yticks(list(y_positions))
ax.set_yticklabels([TARGET_LABELS[t] for t in availability["target"]])
ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.YearLocator())
ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%Y"))
style_axis(ax)
ax.grid(axis="x", color="#e1e0d9", linewidth=0.8, zorder=0)
ax.set_title("Data availability vs. train / validation / test split", pad=45)
ax.legend(loc="lower center", ncol=4, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.02))
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(paths.images_path / "03_data_availability.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")

records.content:
30-day rolling standard deviation of each headline variable — a way to
see which periods are more or less volatile, not just what the level
is. For pv/wind this mixes two effects: the diurnal on/off cycle’s own
amplitude (which itself varies seasonally — e.g. PV swings harder on long
summer days than short winter ones) and genuine day-to-day weather
variability, so a high value here doesn’t by itself mean “stormier
weather” — only that the series moved around more, for whichever reason.



Figure 3:30-day rolling standard deviation of each headline variable, full history.

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 8), sharex=True)

for ax, target in zip(axes.flat, TARGETS):
    # min_periods=15 days: without it, the window's first few hours produce
    # noisy std estimates from a handful of points, showing up as a sharp
    # spike right at the start of each series.
    rolling_std = panel[target].rolling("30D", min_periods=24 * 15).std()
    ax.plot(rolling_std.index, rolling_std, color=TARGET_COLORS[target], linewidth=0.8)
    ax.set_title(TARGET_LABELS[target])
    ax.set_ylabel("30d rolling std (MW)")
    style_axis(ax)

fig.suptitle("Headline variables — 30-day rolling volatility", y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(paths.images_path / "03_rolling_volatility.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

records.content:
For each calendar day-of-year (Jan 1 .. Dec 31), pool every hourly
observation that falls on that day across all years in the panel and take
their standard deviation — a climatological view of which times of year
are typically more volatile. This complements the rolling-30-day chart
above: that one shows the actual volatility trajectory over time (trend
and season mixed together), this one averages out year-to-year
differences and isolates the pure seasonal shape.



Figure 4:Standard deviation of each headline variable’s hourly values, pooled by
day-of-year across all years in the panel.

doy_std = panel.groupby(panel.index.dayofyear)[TARGETS].std()
# Map day-of-year (1..366) onto a placeholder non-leap year's dates so the
# x-axis can use real month labels — these aren't real observation dates.
doy_dates = pd.Timestamp("2001-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(doy_std.index - 1, unit="D")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 8), sharex=True)

for ax, target in zip(axes.flat, TARGETS):
    ax.plot(doy_dates, doy_std[target], color=TARGET_COLORS[target], linewidth=1.2)
    ax.set_title(TARGET_LABELS[target])
    ax.set_ylabel("Std by day-of-year (MW)")
    ax.xaxis.set_major_locator(mdates.MonthLocator())
    ax.xaxis.set_major_formatter(mdates.DateFormatter("%b"))
    style_axis(ax)

fig.suptitle("Headline variables — standard deviation by day-of-year", y=1.02)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(paths.images_path / "03_doy_std.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

records.content:
Stacked PV + wind onshore + wind offshore generation against load — the
big-picture view of renewable buildout catching up to demand over the
years. Daily means, since the full multi-year history at hourly
resolution would just be visual noise — but that averaging also hides
exactly the moments this chart alone can’t show: at hourly resolution,
renewables actually exceed load in 602 of the ~87,600 hours in this
panel, none of which are visible here since a single high hour gets
averaged into its day. See the next chart for that.



Figure 5:Daily-mean stacked renewable generation (PV, wind onshore, wind offshore)
vs. daily-mean load, full history.

daily = panel[TARGETS].resample("D").mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 5))

ax.stackplot(
    daily.index,
    daily["pv"],
    daily["wind_onshore"],
    daily["wind_offshore"],
    colors=[TARGET_COLORS["pv"], TARGET_COLORS["wind_onshore"], TARGET_COLORS["wind_offshore"]],
    labels=[TARGET_LABELS["pv"], TARGET_LABELS["wind_onshore"], TARGET_LABELS["wind_offshore"]],
    alpha=0.85,
    zorder=2,
)
ax.plot(daily.index, daily["load"], color=ACTUAL_COLOR, linewidth=1.2, label=TARGET_LABELS["load"], zorder=3)

ax.set_ylabel("MW (daily mean)")
ax.set_title("Stacked renewable generation vs. load")
style_axis(ax)
ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=4, frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 1.14))
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(paths.images_path / "03_renewables_vs_demand.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

records.content:
Daily maximum (not mean) of the hourly renewable/load ratio — preserves
the within-day peak instead of averaging it away, so hours where
renewables actually cover all of load (ratio >= 1, above the reference
line) are visible as spikes. Even ratios comfortably below 1 are still
curtailment-risk candidates in practice: Germany’s inflexible (“must-run”)
baseload generation can’t ramp down to zero, so once renewables cover
most of residual demand, wind/solar is usually the cheapest thing left
to curtail — not just literal renewables > load moments. Not a direct
curtailment measurement either way (see the note above), but a much more
honest “candidate periods” view than the daily-mean chart above.



Figure 6:Daily maximum of the hourly (PV + wind onshore + wind offshore) / load
ratio, full history. The dashed line marks 100% (renewables alone
covering all of that hour’s load).

renewable_share = (panel["pv"] + panel["wind_onshore"] + panel["wind_offshore"]) / panel["load"]
daily_peak_share = renewable_share.resample("D").max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 4.5))
ax.plot(daily_peak_share.index, daily_peak_share * 100, color=TARGET_COLORS["wind_onshore"], linewidth=0.8)
ax.axhline(100, color=ACTUAL_COLOR, linewidth=1, linestyle="--", zorder=3)
ax.set_ylabel("Daily peak renewable\nshare of load (%)")
ax.set_title("Renewable share of load — daily peak hour")
style_axis(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
fig.savefig(paths.images_path / "03_renewable_share_of_load.png", dpi=150, bbox_inches="tight")
plt.show()

records.content:
One LinearRegression (on standardized features, via a
StandardScaler pipeline — needed so coefficient magnitude is a
meaningful importance signal later, without changing the predictions
themselves) per (target, horizon) cell, trained on data before the
validation cutoff and scored on the validation period only (test is
reserved — see docs/modeling_plan.md).

def make_model():
    return make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LinearRegression())


def importance_fn(model, feature_names):
    coefs = model.named_steps["linearregression"].coef_
    return pd.Series(np.abs(coefs), index=feature_names)


results, val_predictions, importances = fit_and_evaluate(panel, make_model, importance_fn)

save_scenario_metrics(
    paths,
    scenario_id=SCENARIO_ID,
    title=MODEL_LABEL,
    description=(
        "Linear regression (standardized features) on seasonality (daily/annual) + "
        "short lags (1h, 2h, 24h, 48h) + load-only weekday features. No weather/capacity data."
    ),
    notebook="04_baseline_linear_regression",
    valid=True,
    results=results,
)
print(f"Saved -> {paths.scenario_results_file(SCENARIO_ID)}")

        n_estimators=300,
        max_depth=6,
        learning_rate=0.05,
        random_state=42,
        verbose=-1,
        importance_type="gain",

def importance_fn(model, feature_names):
    return pd.Series(model.feature_importances_, index=feature_names)

    paths,
    scenario_id=SCENARIO_ID,

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from dhf.paths import ProjPaths
from dhf.scenarios import load_all_scenario_metrics
from dhf.viz import TARGET_LABELS, assign_scenario_colors, style_axis

paths = ProjPaths()
paths.ensure_directories()

TARGETS = ["pv", "wind_onshore", "wind_offshore", "load"]

metrics = load_all_scenario_metrics(paths)
horizons_days = sorted(metrics["horizon_days"].unique())
scenario_titles = metrics.drop_duplicates("scenario_id").set_index("scenario_id")["title"]
scenario_colors = assign_scenario_colors(sorted(metrics["scenario_id"].unique()))

print(f"{len(scenario_colors)} scenarios: {list(scenario_colors)}")



def plot_metric_by_horizon(metric: str) -> plt.Figure:
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 8))
    for ax, target in zip(axes.flat, TARGETS):
        target_metrics = metrics[metrics["target"] == target]
        for scenario_id, group in target_metrics.groupby("scenario_id"):
            group = group.sort_values("horizon_days")
            ax.plot(
                group["horizon_days"],
                group[metric],
                color=scenario_colors[scenario_id],
                marker="o",
                linewidth=2,
                label=scenario_titles[scenario_id],
                zorder=3,
            )
        ax.set_xticks(horizons_days)
        ax.set_xticklabels([f"{h}d" for h in horizons_days])
        ax.set_title(TARGET_LABELS[target])
        ax.set_ylabel(f"Validation {metric.upper()} (MW)")
        ax.set_ylim(bottom=0)
        style_axis(ax)

    handles, labels = axes.flat[0].get_legend_handles_labels()
    fig.legend(handles, labels, loc="upper center", ncol=len(scenario_colors), bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.04), frameon=False)
    fig.tight_layout()
    return fig

records.content:
PECD v4.2 does not offer NUTS-level spatial aggregation for wind capacity
factors (unlike solar, which has clean NUTS2 coverage) — only two
pan-European zone schemes: PEON (onshore) and PEOF (offshore). Germany
intersects 7 PEON zones (DE01..DE07) and 6 PEOF zones (DE011..DE015,
DE02). See docs/data_sources.md.

The zone boundaries aren’t published as a shapefile, but the CDS “weights
and masks” widget provides the same information rasterized: a 0.25 degree
grid where each cell carries its fractional area coverage (0..1) for every
zone (downloaded by pipeline/08_download_pecd_masks.py). This notebook
turns that raster back into vector polygons and plots them against
Germany’s real NUTS2 boundaries, purely as a sanity check — if the zones
look sensible, they become a candidate grouping key for MaStR wind
capacity data (instead of NUTS2, which isn’t an option for wind here).

import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from shapely.geometry import box
from shapely.ops import unary_union

from dhf.paths import ProjPaths
from dhf.viz import FIXED_CATEGORICAL_ORDER

paths = ProjPaths()

GRID_RESOLUTION_DEG = 0.25
COVERAGE_THRESHOLD = 0.5  # a cell "belongs" to a zone once the zone covers >50% of it

records.content:
For each German zone, keep the grid cells the zone covers by more than
COVERAGE_THRESHOLD and dissolve them into one (multi)polygon. This is a
coarse, 0.25 degree-resolution approximation of the true ENTSO-E zone
boundary — good enough to sanity-check shape and placement, not for
precise area calculations.

def zones_from_mask(mask_file, scheme: str, region_suffix: str = "") -> gpd.GeoDataFrame:
    """Polygonize a CDS region mask's German zones into a GeoDataFrame.

    `region_suffix` strips a fixed suffix (e.g. "_OFF") off the raw region
    codes for a cleaner `zone_id` column.
    """
    ds = xr.open_dataset(mask_file)
    de_regions = sorted(r for r in ds.region.values.tolist() if str(r).startswith("DE"))

    half = GRID_RESOLUTION_DEG / 2
    lats, lons = ds.latitude.values, ds.longitude.values
    rows = []
    for region in de_regions:
        covered = (ds["mask"].sel(region=region) > COVERAGE_THRESHOLD).values  # (lat, lon) bool
        lat_idx, lon_idx = np.nonzero(covered)
        boxes = [
            box(lons[j] - half, lats[i] - half, lons[j] + half, lats[i] + half) for i, j in zip(lat_idx, lon_idx)
        ]
        zone_id = region[: -len(region_suffix)] if region_suffix else region
        rows.append({"zone_id": zone_id, "scheme": scheme, "n_cells": len(boxes), "geometry": unary_union(boxes)})
    ds.close()
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame(rows, crs="EPSG:4326")


onshore_zones = zones_from_mask(paths.peon_mask_file, scheme="onshore")
offshore_zones = zones_from_mask(paths.peof_mask_file, scheme="offshore", region_suffix="_OFF")

wind_zones = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    pd.concat([onshore_zones, offshore_zones], ignore_index=True),
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
wind_zones["area_km2"] = wind_zones.to_crs("EPSG:3035").geometry.area / 1e6

print(wind_zones[["zone_id", "scheme", "n_cells", "area_km2"]].to_string(index=False))



wind_zones.to_file(paths.pecd_wind_zones_file, driver="GeoJSON")
print(f"Saved {len(wind_zones)} zones -> {paths.pecd_wind_zones_file}")

records.content:
First feature (see docs/modeling_plan.md): for each of pv, wind_onshore,
wind_offshore, aggregate PECD’s zone-level capacity factors to one
DE-LU-wide, capacity-weighted time series — weights are MaStR’s installed
capacity per region/zone, updated monthly (NUTS2 for solar, PEON/PEOF for
wind, since v4.2 doesn’t offer NUTS2 for wind — see docs/data_sources.md).
Multiplying by total installed capacity gives an implied generation
figure (MW), directly comparable to SMARD’s actual generation.

This is a perfect-foresight sanity check with zero modeling involved: if
PECD’s weather-driven capacity factors and MaStR’s capacity figures
already track actual generation closely on their own, that’s a strong
early signal for CLAUDE.md’s phase 2 (does weather have explanatory
power at all, before any model tries to use it).

CF_AND_CAPACITY = {

implied = {}
for target, (cf, capacity) in CF_AND_CAPACITY.items():

    capacity_national = national_capacity_mw(capacity, cf.index)

comparisons = {}
metrics = []
for target in TARGETS:
    df = pd.concat([target_panel[target].rename("actual"), implied[target].rename("implied")], axis=1, sort=False).dropna()
    comparisons[target] = df
    error = df["implied"] - df["actual"]

            "target": target,

            "end": df.index.max(),

            "mean_actual_mw": mean_actual,
            "mean_implied_mw": df["implied"].mean(),
            "mae_mw": error.abs().mean(),
            "mae_pct_of_mean": error.abs().mean() / mean_actual * 100,
            "bias_mw": error.mean(),
            "bias_pct_of_mean": error.mean() / mean_actual * 100,
            "rmse_mw": (error**2).mean() ** 0.5,

Identical model and baseline feature set as 05_baseline_lightgbm.ipynb
(same LightGBM hyperparameters, same lags/seasonality features), plus two
extra features per technology — PECD v4.2’s capacity-weighted national
capacity factor and MaStR’s total installed capacity, both assumed
perfectly known at the forecast horizon (see
pipeline/12_pecd_mastr_comparison_eda.ipynb for how closely that
perfect-foresight assumption already tracks actual generation on its own,
with no model at all). pv/wind_onshore/wind_offshore each get only their
own technology’s pair; load gets all three — it has no capacity factor
of its own, but PV output in particular plausibly suppresses
grid-visible load through behind-the-meter self-consumption (a household
using its own solar power draws less from the grid), so it’s a candidate
feature worth letting the model test rather than assuming away.

load also gets 2m temperature at country level (temperature_de_c) —
the classic load driver, and the only variable here that isn’t a
capacity factor (see docs/data_sources.md for why population-weighted
temperature isn’t usable at Germany’s specific level in v4.2).

Since real weather/capacity aren’t actually known this far in advance,
this scenario is saved with valid=False (see dhf/scenarios.py) — it
answers “does weather help if known perfectly”, the phase-2 question
from CLAUDE.md, not “would this work operationally” (that’s phase 3).

(name kept for continuity with earlier iterations of this scenario — the
actual refit cadence below is 6 equal-length periods, not literal
calendar quarters; see dhf.reporting.periodic_windows.)

Identical features, model, and hyperparameters as
13_perfect_foresight_weather_lightgbm.ipynb — the only thing that
changes is the refit schedule: instead of one model fit on the
pre-validation training set and scored across the whole ~2-year
validation period, the model is refit 6 times (~4-month windows) on
an expanding window (all data strictly before that window), and only used
to predict that one window (see dhf.reporting.fit_and_evaluate_walkforward).

Motivation: 13_perfect_foresight_weather_lightgbm.ipynb’s scatter plot
showed a hard ceiling in offshore wind predictions — LightGBM (a
tree-based model) can’t predict beyond the range of target values it saw
during training, and offshore capacity nearly tripled over the data’s
history, so a model trained once on a stale multi-year window
systematically under-predicts once the fleet grows past what training
ever saw. Periodic refitting keeps the training window’s upper end closer
to “now,” which should shrink (not necessarily eliminate — see
docs/modeling_plan.md’s note on the target-rescaling alternative, not
applied here) that gap.

This is a refit-schedule-only change relative to
13_perfect_foresight_weather_lightgbm.ipynb — the target is still
absolute MW, not a capacity-factor ratio (that’s a separate, not-yet-tried
lever, deliberately not combined with this one so the two can’t be
confused — see docs/modeling_plan.md’s “one delta at a time” convention).
